**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been asked to decide between two paths: purchasing additional local GPU hardware to meet growing inference demand, or investing engineering time to raise utilisation on the fleet we already own. After several weeks of measurement and modelling, we recommend the second option — improving utilisation first — with a purchase decision deferred until we have better evidence about where our demand curve is actually heading. Here is the reasoning, including where we could be wrong.

Start with cost. Our current fleet of eight A100-class cards runs at roughly 22% average utilisation, with peaks near 60% during afternoon batch windows and troughs near 5% overnight. That is a poor return on capital we have already spent, and it means the marginal value of another card is low relative to the marginal value of engineering effort. A new node costs approximately £180k all-in once you include networking, rack power, and cooling headroom. By contrast, the utilisation work — batching improvements, a proper request queue, model consolidation so we stop serving three fine-tunes of the same base model, and scheduled jobs moved into off-peak windows — is roughly two engineers for six weeks. Even at fully loaded cost, that is an order of magnitude cheaper, and it compounds: every improvement we make now also improves whatever hardware we eventually buy.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side, and we take it seriously. Our p99 latency for interactive requests is 340ms; the target is 250ms. The utilisation work does not automatically fix this, because latency under load depends on tail behaviour, not averages. Better batching can actually *worsen* p99 if we batch too aggressively, and a shared queue introduces contention risk. However, our measurements suggest the current latency problem is driven less by raw capacity than by cold-start model swaps — we evict models from VRAM to make room for others, and those reloads account for an estimated 60% of tail-latency incidents. Fixing eviction policy and pinning the two hottest models is a latency win that requires no new hardware. If, after that work, p99 remains above target under realistic load, that becomes a concrete, quantified trigger for a purchase rather than a guess.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy, and right now a single node failure removes 25% of our capacity, which is uncomfortable. But utilisation work improves reliability too, in a less obvious way: consolidating models and standardising the serving path reduces configuration drift, and a well-instrumented queue gives us graceful degradation under overload instead of silent timeouts. We should also be honest that our reliability incidents in the last quarter were mostly software — a bad weight update, a driver mismatch — not capacity shortfalls. Buying more machines would not have prevented any of them.

Opportunity cost deserves explicit attention. The two engineers who would do the utilisation work are the same people best placed to build the fine-tuning pipeline the research team has been waiting on. If we buy hardware instead, we spend money and still pull those engineers onto integration and rack setup for several weeks, so the opportunity cost is paid either way. The difference is that the utilisation path produces durable capability — better serving infrastructure that benefits every future model — while the purchase path produces capacity that may sit idle if demand shifts, which history suggests it will. Our traffic forecast has been revised downward twice this year.

Finally, reversibility. Buying hardware is close to irreversible at our scale: depreciation is fast, resale is poor, and the commitment shapes our power and networking footprint for years. Utilisation work is almost entirely reversible — we can change batching policy, queue design, and model placement as we learn. When one option locks us in and the other keeps options open, and the reversible option is also cheaper, the decision framework points clearly in one direction.

What would change our minds: if interactive demand grows faster than 15% month-over-month for two consecutive months, or if the eviction and batching work fails to bring p99 under 300ms by the end of the quarter, we should revisit the purchase immediately, with a specific ask for two nodes rather than a full rack. We also acknowledge uncertainty in our own measurements — utilisation figures come from a sampling agent with known blind spots during driver resets, and our demand forecast is based on three months of data. We will re-baseline both before the mid-quarter review.

Recommendation: fund the utilisation project now, set explicit latency and demand triggers for a hardware purchase, and revisit at the end of Q3 with numbers rather than instincts.
